post.title: Agent Sessions: One macOS Cockpit for Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI History
post.description: Inside Agent Sessions, Alexander Malakhov's native macOS app that unifies Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI history, search, resume, and rate limits.
post.excerpt: Every AI coding agent buries its session history in a different hidden format. Agent Sessions, a native macOS app by Alexander Malakhov, puts cross-tool search, resume, and rate-limit tracking in one place. I forked it to study the source, and this post is what I found.
post.content:
I run three coding agents most days: Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. Each one keeps its session history in its own format, in its own hidden directory. Finding a prompt I wrote last Tuesday means grepping JSONL across half a dozen dotfolders, assuming I even remember which agent I was talking to.

Agent Sessions fixes this. It is a native macOS app (Swift/SwiftUI, MIT licensed) that gives you one browser, one search box, and one resume button across roughly a dozen agent CLIs, plus live rate-limit tracking for Claude and Codex. As an Agentic Engineer I live inside these tools all day, and this app has earned a permanent spot in my menu bar.

One thing before anything else: **I did not build this.** Agent Sessions is the work of Alexander Malakhov, published as [jazzyalex/agent-sessions](https://github.com/jazzyalex/agent-sessions) on GitHub. I forked it in May to study the source, and this post is that study written up. Install from his tap, star his repo. My fork's only contribution to this story is an embarrassing lesson I will get to at the end.

## The problem: every agent hides its history differently

Codex writes JSONL to `~/.codex/sessions`. Claude Code writes to `~/.claude/sessions`. Gemini CLI dumps into `~/.gemini/tmp`. Copilot keeps `~/.copilot/session-state`. Cursor and Factory use their own directories. OpenCode skips JSONL entirely and writes a SQLite database at `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`.

Across that mess there are three things you cannot do: search a past prompt or tool output across tools, reconstruct the exact CLI command that resumes a specific session, and check how close you are to your Claude or Codex rate limits without opening each CLI and asking.

Agent Sessions does all three in one app. Per its README and privacy docs, it reads each agent's directories in read-only mode and never sends session data off the machine. The only network activity is optional Sparkle update checks.

## Install

```bash
brew tap jazzyalex/agent-sessions && brew install --cask agent-sessions
```

Note the tap: that is the original author's Homebrew tap, where the releases actually live. He also ships a signed and notarized DMG with Sparkle 2 auto-updates. macOS 14+ required.

## How it works

I spent real time in the source, so here is the architecture as it exists in the code, not the marketing version.

1. **Per-agent indexers, read-only.** Every agent gets its own parser module: `SessionIndexer` for Codex, `ClaudeSessionIndexer` for Claude, plus Hermes, Pi, Cursor, Copilot, and Droid modules. A `UnifiedSessionIndexer` aggregates them into one session list with strict per-agent filtering. Coverage spans Codex (CLI, Desktop, VS Code), Claude (CLI, Desktop), Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Hermes, and OpenClaw, with Pi as tier-2. The module tree is essentially a multi-dialect parser museum for agent session formats.

2. **Progressive two-phase search.** Sessions exist in two states: lightweight (id, path, timestamps, model, file size) and fully parsed (the complete JSONL event array). On a query, the `SearchCoordinator` partitions sessions at a 10MB threshold. Small and medium files get scanned in batches of 64 with on-the-fly parsing. The 10MB-plus monsters are parsed sequentially, one at a time, to avoid memory spikes. Click a session mid-scan and a promotion mechanism parses it immediately. Parsed results get written back into the canonical `allSessions` arrays, so the work survives after the search clears. The whole design is documented in `docs/search-architecture.md`.

3. **A local SQLite index.** An actor-wrapped SQLite3 database (`IndexDB`, stored at `Application Support/AgentSessions/index.db`) holds file scan state, per-session daily metrics, and day rollups for the analytics views. SQLite via the C API, wrapped in a Swift actor for thread safety. It is the same local-first pattern I keep reaching for in my own tools.

4. **Rate limits, two opposite strategies.** This is the most technically interesting part. Claude CLI exposes no passive usage logs, so `ClaudeStatusService` drives a real tmux session running the `claude` binary and types `/usage` into it through a bash capture script, polling every 15 minutes. It imports `IOKit.ps` to check power state, slows down on battery, and stops entirely when the UI is hidden. Codex needs none of that theater: `CodexCLIRPCProbe` sends a JSON-RPC initialize handshake over stdin/stdout and calls `account/rateLimits/read`. The code comment reads "No tmux, no PTY." Two CLIs, same job, opposite reverse-engineering strategies. That gap is a tidy snapshot of how un-standardized the agent-CLI ecosystem still is.

5. **Agent Cockpit (beta).** A live menu-bar command center that groups your active iTerm2 sessions for Codex, Claude, and OpenCode, with active/waiting summaries and a live Claude usage strip: the 5-hour session window, weekly all-models, and weekly Opus, shown as percent remaining.

6. **Resume by reconstruction.** Right-click a session and Copy Resume Command gives you the exact per-agent invocation, or the app opens it directly in Terminal.app or iTerm2. Equivalents exist for Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Copilot.

The generated resume commands look like this:

```bash
claude --resume <uuid>   # only works when cwd matches the project root
gemini --resume <id>
pi --session
```

## Building from source

The repo is a standard Xcode project with a SwiftLint config:

```bash
xcodebuild -project AgentSessions.xcodeproj -scheme AgentSessions -configuration Debug -destination 'platform=macOS' build
```

Tests:

```bash
xcodebuild -project AgentSessions.xcodeproj -scheme AgentSessionsTests -destination 'platform=macOS' test
```

And if you want to force a Sparkle update check on an installed copy:

```bash
defaults delete com.triada.AgentSessions SULastCheckTime && open "/Applications/Agent Sessions.app"
```

One detail from the repo that made me smile: its `CLAUDE.md` bans AI co-authorship outright. "All commits MUST be authored by the repository owner only. Never add Claude as a co-author." An AI-session browser that keeps AI out of its own author field.

## Honest limitations

- **The big one, again: this is not my project.** My fork (`aryateja2106/agent-sessions`) has zero original commits. Every line is Malakhov's. The stars, the releases, and the Homebrew tap all belong to upstream.
- **Tracking your quota can spend your quota.** The Claude `/usage` probe launches Claude Code through tmux, and the code explicitly warns it "may count toward Claude Code usage limits." Claude has no passive usage logs, so polling is the only option.
- **It is not real-time.** Polling runs every 15 minutes, with documented staleness windows: 90 minutes for the session window, 6 hours for the weekly numbers.
- **It is not fully offline.** Sparkle update checks are optional network activity, and the rate-limit probes launch vendor CLIs that talk to their vendors' servers.
- macOS 14+ only. No Windows, no Linux.
- Agent Cockpit is beta and iTerm2-only. Resume and cockpit flows target Terminal.app and iTerm2.
- `claude --resume` only works when your cwd matches the project root.
- Pi CLI support is explicitly tier-2.

## What's next

Here is the embarrassing lesson. I forked this repo on May 22 to study it. Today my fork is 0 commits ahead and 435 commits behind upstream. Seven weeks of not pulling, and a fast-moving agent-tooling repo left my copy in the graveyard. If you fork to learn, either sync on a schedule or read from a fresh clone. A stale fork is worse than no fork, because it looks like a claim.

What I am actually taking from this codebase: the per-agent parser-module layout, the actor-wrapped SQLite pattern for local indexing, and the two-phase search partition trick. Those patterns will show up in my own tooling. The app itself stays installed from jazzyalex's tap, where the credit belongs.
